clue.text: Name penned by royal chap, say, in old-fashioned correspondence?

indicators.note: penned by means held inside, as if shut in a pen, so the abbreviation goes inside the sail

parts.note: a royal is a small sail set high on a square-rigged ship's mast

indicators.note: say signals that the next word is only to be heard, not spelt

parts.note: a chap is a man, a male

explanation.surface: A letter from a prince, written in the old style, with someone's name inked in by hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'royal' looks royal but is a sailing term. 'say' tells you MALE (a chap) is to be heard and spelt MAIL.
explanation.definitionFit: Slow letters sent through the postal service are jokingly contrasted with email, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Charitable donations raised around one state capital

indicators.note: around means the reversed word goes round the letter for one
raised in a down clue means the word is read upwards, back to front

parts.note: alms are charitable gifts to the poor
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Gifts to charity are collected around a state capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' turns ALMS into SMLA, which goes round I.
explanation.definitionFit: Simla, now spelt Shimla, is the capital of the Indian state of Himachal Pradesh.

clue.text: Senior officer in late danger, junta being corrupt

indicators.note: corrupt means spoilt or altered, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A senior officer faces danger from a corrupt military junta.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being corrupt' rearranges LATE DANGER JUNTA, taken as written.
explanation.definitionFit: A high-ranking army staff officer responsible for personnel and administration holds this title.

clue.text: Democrat always seen with parliamentarians on Christian Sabbath

indicators.note: seen with places the democrat's letter alongside, before the word for always and after the peers

parts.note: the Lords are members of the upper house of the UK Parliament
ay, also spelt aye, is an old word for always

explanation.surface: An American Democrat joins British peers for Sunday worship.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunday, the Christian day of rest and worship, is traditionally called this.

clue.text: Vocal part provided by composer of Belshazzar's Feast

indicators.note: provided by says the part is supplied from within the composer's name, its outer letters dropped

parts.note: Belshazzar's Feast is a choral work by the English composer William Walton

explanation.surface: A singer's line in a famous English oratorio.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter means the part sits inside WALTON; drop its first and last letters, W and N.
explanation.definitionFit: The alto is the lower female or high male voice part in a choir.

clue.text: So-called active gangland member's source of income

indicators.note: so-called signals a sound-alike, the words as named or spoken

parts.note: lively means active, and a hood is a gangster

explanation.surface: A busy mobster's earnings come from crime.
explanation.walkthrough: A HOOD is a gangster. Said aloud, LIVELY HOOD sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: One's livelihood is the means of earning a living, a source of income.

clue.text: Was a model faced with no work?

indicators.note: no tells you the work is taken away from the longer word

parts.note: to be faced with something is to be opposed by it
OP is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether an unemployed person ended up sitting for an artist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no' removes OP from OPPOSED, leaving the definition's verb.
explanation.definitionFit: An artist's model sits or stands still in position for the painter, which is to pose.

clue.text: Take off gun when taking wages round

indicators.note: round means the wages go round the gun

parts.note: pay means wages
rod is American slang for a gun

explanation.surface: A robber takes off with a gun while the payroll is being delivered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take off' looks like escaping; it means mimic.
explanation.definitionFit: To take off someone is to mimic them, which is what a parody does.

clue.text: Hearty cry from very shirty member is out of order

indicators.note: out of order means jumbled, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone yells at a very bad-tempered club member who has broken the rules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shirty' is British slang for bad-tempered. A 'hearty' is a sailor, so the cry is a stage pirate's oath.
explanation.definitionFit: A hearty is a jolly sailor, and this mock oath is the stock exclamation of fictional old seamen.

clue.text: Turned up without practical means to cause explosion

indicators.note: without means outside, so the reversed word goes around the other piece
up in a down clue means the word is read upwards, back to front

parts.note: turned means rotated
on means practicable or feasible, as in 'that's not on'

explanation.surface: Someone appears without any practical way of setting off a blast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns ROTATED into DETATOR. 'Turned up' reads as arrived, a false path.
explanation.definitionFit: A detonator is the device that sets off an explosive charge.

clue.text: In any case this decision won't be reached by five to seven

definitions.text: In any case this decision won't be reached by five to seven

parts.words: In any case this decision won't be reached by five to seven
parts.note: a 'case' is a court trial; a jury of twelve split five against seven is too divided for the accepted kind of decision that does not need unanimity

explanation.surface: A remark that some decision will never be made in the evening hours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'five to seven' reads like a time of day, 6.55, but it is a jury split of 5-7. In English courts a jury may return a verdict 10-2 or 11-1, never 5-7.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description of a jury decision agreed by most jurors rather than all of them.

clue.text: Demonstrate with a time trial

parts.note: a trial is a test

explanation.surface: Someone shows off their cycling form in a race against the clock.
explanation.definitionFit: To attest is to show or bear witness that something is true, much as to demonstrate it.

clue.text: Make concessions about securing entrance to luncheon club

indicators.note: securing means holding something firmly inside, so a letter goes into the word for giving way

parts.note: to budge is to give way or make concessions

indicators.note: entrance to means the opening letter of the word that follows

parts.note: on means about, concerning

explanation.surface: A gentlemen's club relaxes its rules to let guests in for lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'luncheon club' reads as one place; 'club' is the definition, a heavy stick.
explanation.definitionFit: A bludgeon is a short heavy stick used as a weapon, a cudgel or club.

clue.text: How far one might go to steal firearms in practice here

definitions.text: How far one might go to steal
definitions.meaning: to rifle is to steal or ransack, and a range is a distance one might reach
a place where shooters practise with guns

explanation.definitionFit: A shooting ground for target practice with guns, also read as the reach of a thief.

clue.text: Execute, correctly, direction given in New York

parts.note: to hang someone is to execute them
aright is an old-fashioned word for correctly

explanation.surface: Someone tells you how to carry out an execution properly in Manhattan.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is American slang for making a right turn, hence the New York in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: American drivers say they will make a right turn this way, so it is street directions in an American city.

clue.text: Manage pub found in guide for bikers

parts.note: to handle is to manage
a bar is a pub

explanation.surface: Someone runs a pub listed in a guidebook for motorcyclists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'guide for bikers' sounds like a guidebook; it is the part a cyclist steers with.
explanation.definitionFit: The handlebar is the bar a cyclist steers with, which guides the bike.

clue.text: Bird returning to shed

indicators.note: returning means the word is read from back to front

parts.note: bird is British slang for a prison sentence, time served

explanation.surface: A pigeon flies home to its shed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird' looks like a pigeon going back to its loft; it is British slang (doing bird) for a prison sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: To shed something, like light or heat, is to give it off or send it out.

clue.text: Suit and tie — we cop out

indicators.note: out means not in proper order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A suit and tie are worn when the police come for us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges TIE WE COP. 'cop out' reads as a dodge.
explanation.definitionFit: A suit made of jacket and trousers or skirt is named for its two matching parts.

clue.text: Impossible rhymes

definitions.meaning: something not possible or not allowed, out of the question
the two little words of the answer sound alike at their ends

explanation.definitionFit: A situation that cannot happen is called this, and its two halves also happen to rhyme with each other.

clue.text: Excess liquidity left after banks collapse?

definitions.text: Excess liquidity left after banks collapse?

parts.words: Excess liquidity left after banks collapse?
parts.note: reads as finance after a banking crash, but the banks are river banks and the liquidity is real liquid left over when they give way

explanation.surface: Surplus cash floats around after financial institutions crash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'liquidity' and 'banks' are money words; read them literally as water and riverbanks.
explanation.definitionFit: Water spilling over land after a river breaks through its banks is a cryptic picture of overflow.

clue.text: Be first to appear in extremely folkish Irish festival

indicators.note: to appear in means to show up inside, so the word goes into the outer letters
extremely means the first and last letters of the word that follows

parts.note: to lead is to be first

explanation.surface: Someone longs to top the bill at a very folksy Irish music festival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely folkish' looks like very folksy; it gives F and H, the word's first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A fleadh is an Irish or Celtic festival of traditional music and dance.

clue.text: He wants letters but ones under the table he might throw out

definitions.text: He wants letters but ones under the table he might throw out

parts.words: He wants letters but ones under the table he might throw out
parts.note: letters here are lets, properties rented out, and those under the table are drunks a publican ejects

explanation.surface: A man wants post, but he discards anything that arrives under the table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'letters' means properties to rent, not post, and 'under the table' means drunk, not bribery. The same word serves for a property owner and a pub keeper.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a property owner seeking tenants and a pub keeper ejecting drunk customers go by this title.

clue.text: Our predecessors as soldiers on a sort of exercise

indicators.note: on means placed after, the soldiers following the other pieces

parts.note: PE is physical education, exercise at school
men is a common term for soldiers, the ranks

explanation.surface: Ancestors are compared to troops out on a training drill.
explanation.definitionFit: Early hominids, half ape and half man, are imagined as human ancestors.

clue.text: Not all there is of Brazil?

definitions.meaning: a Brazil is a kind of nut, so being of it is jokingly described as nutlike

explanation.definitionFit: Crazy people are called this informally, and the word also describes something tasting of nuts like the Brazil.

clue.text: Mentioned Portuguese navigator's taken northern route

indicators.note: taking a northern route in a down clue means going upwards, so the name is read back to front

parts.note: Bartolomeu Dias was the Portuguese navigator who rounded the Cape of Good Hope

explanation.surface: A remark that a Portuguese explorer sailed north.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that has been said or stated has been mentioned.

clue.text: What's in store for you? A good deal here!

definitions.text: What's in store for you? A good deal here!

parts.words: What's in store for you? A good deal here!
parts.note: 'in store' is literal, inside a shop, and 'a good deal' means a bargain, found on its cheap lowest floor

explanation.surface: A fortune teller promises a lot in your future.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What's in store for you' sounds like fortune telling; it is the bottom floor of a department store where goods are sold cheaply.
explanation.definitionFit: The cheap lowest floor of a department store, where cut-price goods are sold, is described cryptically.

clue.text: Fellow's contribution to moral philosophy

indicators.note: contribution to says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A college fellow's essay on ethics.
explanation.definitionFit: A man's first name stands for any fellow, a common crossword convention for male names.

clue.text: Lease written so offering meadows in perpetuity

annotationWithheld.why: Lease written so offering meadows in perpetuity (9): a reverse clue whose reading ENDLESS+LY is an instruction on the whole phrase ('Lease' written without its end gives LEAS, meadows); reverse over a 3+ word phrase is refused (reverse_phrase) and cd is refused as a downgrade
annotationWithheld.clue: Lease written so offering meadows in perpetuity
